scope: Learning-psychology evidence for project-authored Grade 3 action analysis

sources.citation: Fuchs et al. (2021). Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades. WWC 2021006.
sources.verifiedSections: Recommendations 1 (printed pp. 5–10), 2 (11–20), 3 (21–28), 5 (40–50); PDF physical pages = printed page + 6
sources.population: Elementary grades, especially students struggling with mathematics; not an experimental validation of this project’s Korean Grade 3 designs.
sources.sourceFinding: Guide rates systematic instruction, precise mathematical language, and concrete/semi-concrete representations as strong-evidence recommendations. Recommendations concern instructional bundles, not proof of each micro-action.
sources.applicationInference: Use concise modeling, response checks, contingent feedback, explicit representation-to-symbol links and need-based support reduction.
limits: Intervention populations and US contexts differ from a Korean general Grade 3 class.
The guide is not a fixed recipe; no local learning-effect claim is justified.
Does not establish a mandatory concrete→pictorial→abstract sequence for every child or concept.

sources.citation: Pashler et al. (2007). Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning.
sources.population: Broad content-learning settings and subjects; not specific to Korean Grade 3.
sources.sourceFinding: Rates alternating worked examples and problems and integrating concrete/abstract representations as moderate evidence; explanatory questioning as strong evidence.
sources.applicationInference: Place example study next to a structurally related student attempt; ask a focused why-question at a mathematically meaningful junction.
limits: Recommendation-level strength must not be copied as an effect-size claim for the current worksheet.
Explanatory questions require accessible prerequisites and response support.

sources.citation: Rittle-Johnson, B. (2006). Promoting Transfer: Effects of Self-Explanation and Direct Instruction. Child Development, 77(1), 1–15.
sources.verifiedSections: Abstract p. 1; conceptual results p. 9; discussion p. 10; limitations pp. 11–12
sources.population: 85 children in grades 3–5, ages 8–11; mathematical equivalence; instruction/invention × explanation/no explanation.
sources.sourceFinding: Self-explanation supported procedural learning and transfer, retained at a two-week delay. Direct instruction supported learning/retention of correct procedures. Neither intervention improved the independent conceptual measure more than comparison conditions.
sources.applicationInference: Ask students to connect a specific action to a relation, while checking explanation content rather than treating speech quantity as understanding.
limits: Equivalence findings do not directly establish effects in multiplication, remainder division, or circle geometry.
Invention conditions had limited time and resources.
A correct answer, a fluent sentence, or an adult-like explanation is not sufficient evidence of concept mastery.

sources.citation: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The Use of Worked Examples as a Substitute for Problem Solving in Learning Algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59–89.
sources.verifiedSections: Publisher abstract; no claim of full-text verification
sources.population: Algebra; experiment 1 included Year 9, Year 11 and university mathematics students. This is not Grade 3 arithmetic evidence.
sources.sourceFinding: Worked-example conditions showed faster solving and fewer errors on subsequent structurally identical problems; generalization was constrained.
sources.applicationInference: Treat worked examples as a way to reduce unguided search for novices; make necessary relations visible instead of requiring simultaneous discovery and calculation.
limits: Cognitive-load account is a theoretical rationale, not a measured load reduction in this project.
Do not infer wide transfer or preschool/Grade 3 effect sizes from this study.

sources.citation: Renkl, A., Atkinson, R. K., Maier, U. H., & Staley, R. (2002). From Example Study to Problem Solving: Smooth Transitions Help Learning. Journal of Experimental Education, 70(4), 293–315.
sources.verifiedSections: Author institution abstract; sample context cross-checked through ERIC EJ658398
sources.population: Ninth-grade and college learners; field and laboratory experiments, not Grade 3.
sources.sourceFinding: Gradually incomplete worked examples benefited near transfer; backward fading was more favorable than forward fading in the investigated settings.
sources.applicationInference: After observed readiness, remove one answer/location cue and ask the learner to complete that part before independent solving.
limits: Do not prescribe backward fading for every Grade 3 mathematical decision.
Any local readiness threshold is a project design rule, not a threshold validated by this study.
